card.questionText: Discuss in detail the importance of any two of the following in maintaining a positive health and safety culture among workers on a construction site: safety training; health and safety officer; risk assessment audit.

rows.verbatim: The importance of any two in maintaining a positive health and safety culture
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, 6 each, discussing why each matters to a positive health and safety culture. Safety training: Safe Pass is mandatory and kept current through refresher courses; training builds awareness of site risks and the skills to identify them and follow best practice; specialist tickets for machinery and vehicles; monitoring and enforcing safe work practices; it may be a condition of the insurance provider. Health and safety officer: provides induction and ongoing training (working at heights, machinery use); develops emergency response plans; keeps first aid and emergency equipment available; ensures the correct PPE is worn; carries out safety inspections and risk assessments; reviews the safety statement; investigates, records and reports accidents. Risk assessment audit: provides a safe working environment; evaluates compliance with safety regulations and policies; identifies hazards and puts control measures in place where a risk cannot be eliminated (for fire: alarms, evacuation signage, drills, extinguishers); recommends improvements; identifies training needs; reduces accidents and liability.

card.stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1970s is of single leaf hollow-block construction with an external render. Insulated plasterboard is fixed to the internal surface of the wall. It is proposed to upgrade the thermal properties of the external wall by installing external insulation as shown.
card.questionText: Calculate the U-value of the proposed wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: External acrylic render thickness 8 mm External polystyrene insulation thickness 100 mm External render thickness 16 mm Hollow concrete block thickness 215 mm Insulation thickness 25 mm Plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm Internal skim coat thickness 3 mm. Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of acrylic render (k) 0.670 W/m ºC; Conductivity of external insulation (k) 0.030 W/m ºC; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m ºC/W; Resistance of hollow concrete block (R) 0.210 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.037 W/m ºC; Conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.160 W/m ºC; Resistivity of skim coat (r) 5.550 m ºC/W; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m2 ºC/W.

rows.contextNote: External surface resistance 0.048 m²°C/W (given).
Internal surface resistance 0.122 m²°C/W (given).

Seven layer resistances, 3 each: acrylic render 0.008 ÷ 0.670 = 0.012; external insulation 0.100 ÷ 0.030 = 3.333; sand cement render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; hollow concrete block 0.210 (given); insulation 0.025 ÷ 0.037 = 0.676; plasterboard 0.0125 ÷ 0.160 = 0.078; internal skim coat 0.003 × 5.550 = 0.017 m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 4.531 m²°C/W (sum of all resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 4.531 = 0.221 W/m²°C, with units.

card.stem: An airtight external building envelope is important in the design of a dwelling house.
card.questionText: The drawing shows an outline section of a two-storey house having a 450 mm external concrete block wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity. The house has a truss roof and a first floor of timber construction. The external door has a thermally broken frame. A Mechanical Ventilation with Heat Recovery system supplies ventilation through ceiling ducts. Using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing that will prevent air leakage at any three of the locations circled on the drawing.

rows.verbatim: Best practice design detailing to prevent air leakage at any three of the locations circled
rows.contextNote: Any three of the four circled locations, each notes 8 and sketches 8 = 16, showing the continuous airtight layer. Head of external door: seal the thermally broken door frame to the reveal of the inner block wall with plasterable airtightness tape, then plaster over the tape; or airtightness paint on the reveal before plastering, or slabbing and skimming. First floor junction with external wall: make the wall airtight where the joists bear — an airtightness membrane sealed with airtight silicone or plasterable tape, or sand cement render or airtightness paint; tape each joist where it breaks the airtightness barrier; seal the floor/wall and roof/wall junctions with tape or paint. Wallplate level: an airtightness membrane under the ceiling joists, wrapped onto the wallplate and down onto the first block below it, fixed to the wall with plasterable airtightness tape or a bead of airtight silicone, then scrim or mesh and sand cement plaster. MVHR duct protruding through the ceiling: an airtightness membrane under the joists, sealed to the duct with a self-adhesive grommet fixed to the membrane, or by carefully taping the duct to the membrane with airtightness tape.

card.stem: The sketch shows the proposed design of a Passive House which is to be constructed in a rural setting.
card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following in Passive House design: building form; foundation design; space heating energy demand.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the importance of any two in Passive House design
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Building form: a compact, simple rectangular form with the smallest surface area (A/V ratio 0.7 or less) to cut heat loss, materials and cost; a narrow plan, one room deep, to maximise solar gain; clean lines in walls and roof that make airtightness easy. Foundation design: insulated ring-beam or passive raft foundations wrapped in insulation to eliminate thermal bridging; thermal blocks in the inner-leaf rising wall; 50–100 mm edge insulation at the floor/wall junction; thermally broken wall ties; a U-value of 0.10–0.15 W/m²K. Space heating energy demand: passive house space-heating demand of no more than 15 kWh/m² per year; quality workmanship in airtightness and insulation; eliminating thermal bridges; solar gain through well-designed fenestration; solar shading, thermal mass and controlled ventilation to keep about 20 °C all year.

card.questionText:
(a) Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following in Passive House design: building form; foundation design; space heating energy demand.

(b) Using notes and freehand sketches, suggest a preferred orientation for the house shown. Show the sun path on your sketch. Discuss two benefits to the homeowner of your preferred orientation.

(c) Solar overheating may occur during the summer months in the house shown. Using notes and freehand sketches, suggest two ways to reduce the possibility of solar overheating while respecting the character of this house design.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the importance of any two in Passive House design
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Building form: a compact, simple rectangular form with the smallest surface area (A/V ratio 0.7 or less) to cut heat loss, materials and cost; a narrow plan, one room deep, to maximise solar gain; clean lines in walls and roof that make airtightness easy. Foundation design: insulated ring-beam or passive raft foundations wrapped in insulation to eliminate thermal bridging; thermal blocks in the inner-leaf rising wall; 50–100 mm edge insulation at the floor/wall junction; thermally broken wall ties; a U-value of 0.10–0.15 W/m²K. Space heating energy demand: passive house space-heating demand of no more than 15 kWh/m² per year; quality workmanship in airtightness and insulation; eliminating thermal bridges; solar gain through well-designed fenestration; solar shading, thermal mass and controlled ventilation to keep about 20 °C all year.

card.stem: “The historic built environment is critical in addressing climate change. Protecting, adapting and reusing historic building stock reduces environmental waste and the carbon dioxide emissions associated with demolition and reconstruction. Traditional building methods and materials have much to teach us about the skills needed to work with prevailing weather conditions and the use of available local materials.” Adapted from: Heritage Ireland 2030 Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage Published on: gov.ie/housing
card.questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.contextNote: Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: demolition creates significant waste and carbon dioxide emissions, while reuse conserves timber, stone and brick and avoids new raw-material extraction — the greenest building is the one already built.

rows.verbatim: Discussion Point 2 (5 for point, 5 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: historic buildings used local materials and local knowledge of the climate and prevailing weather, so reuse supports local economies, traditional crafts and skilled jobs.

rows.verbatim: Discussion Point 3 (5 for point, 5 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: reuse preserves local character, vernacular streetscapes and heritage, draws heritage tourism, limits urban sprawl onto green land and can provide homes for those in need. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.
